html:
The 1960 Agadir earthquake struck the Atlantic port of Agadir in Morocco just before midnight on 29 February 1960. It killed at least 12,000 people, about a third of the city's population.

The quake was only moderate, about magnitude 5.8, but it was shallow and centred right under the city. The old kasbah on its hill and the old quarters of stone and mud brick fell in seconds. Few buildings had been built to resist shaking.

Morocco had been independent for only four years. King Mohammed V vowed that Agadir would be rebuilt, and it was, on a new site to the south, with planned streets and modern buildings by leading Moroccan and foreign architects. Morocco's first rules for earthquake-resistant building followed.

The new Agadir grew into a major port and Morocco's leading beach resort. The ruined kasbah hill remains above it. Compare the 2003 Bam earthquake in Iran, another city of mud brick wrecked by a shallow quake.
